title: The Desire of All Nations (Haggai 2:7)
lead: The phrase "the desire of all nations" (KJV, Haggai 2:7) has been read as the nations' treasures, as the Messiah, and as the chosen from the nations. The Hebrew noun is singular and the verb is plural.

sections.b: The Hebrew chemdat kol-haggoyim ("the desire of all the nations") is followed by the plural verb "will come," so most take the noun as collective, "the prized things of all the nations" (the wealth brought to the house, as in Isaiah 60:5-11 and the next verse of Haggai). The Septuagint has "the chosen things of all the nations will come." The Latin Vulgate has "the Desired of all nations will come," and the Latin church read it of Christ. The phrase lives on in Advent: the antiphon "O King of the nations, and their desire," and Charles Wesley's hymn "Come, Thou long-expected Jesus," which says "dear desire of every nation."

Catholic and Lutheran traditions have long read the phrase of Christ; Calvin held to the plural; modern commentators across traditions mostly follow the plural and the nations' wealth. See the "Where Christians differ" card at Haggai 2.
